one_liner: Cloudflare's immutable Rust map/set on a fingerprinting MPHF (2.1-2.7 bits/key); its edge over std HashMap is compactness, not lookup speed.
what_it_does: Builds read-only lookup structures over a fixed key set. Mphf maps each build key to a unique index in 0..n. MapWithDict<K,V> and Set<K> also store the keys so that lookups can reject non-members, and MapWithDict stores each distinct value once in a dictionary. MapWithDictBitpacked<K> bit-packs equal-length Vec<u32> values. You build with TryFrom<HashMap>/TryFrom<HashSet> or from_iter_with_params(iter, gamma) and query with get/contains_key/contains/iter; optional rkyv 0.7 (zero-copy Archived* types with the same lookups) and serde features.
how_it_is_fast: The MPHF is FMPHGO, Beling's 'Fingerprinting-based minimal perfect hashing revisited': keys are hashed with WyHash into a bit array of gamma*n bits per level. A key that lands alone sets its bit, and colliding keys move to the next level. Group optimization splits each level into B-bit groups, tries 2^S seeds per group and keeps the seed with the fewest collisions, so fewer levels are needed (tests at 100k keys: 1.64 average levels at gamma 1.0, 1.06 at gamma 2.0). A query hashes the key once per level until it finds a set bit, then returns rank(bit) from a two-level rank directory (4096/512-bit blocks packed in 16 bytes, ~3.1% overhead, after Kurpicz's rank/select engineering paper). Map and Set then do one equality check against the stored key at that index.
when_to_use: Large static key sets (built offline or at deploy, rebuilt wholesale) where resident memory or cache footprint matters more than per-lookup nanoseconds: the MPHF index costs 2.10-2.72 bits/key, and the key array has no empty slots or control bytes.

Many keys mapped to few distinct values (labels, scores, small enums): MapWithDict stores each distinct value once. MapWithDictBitpacked stores fixed-length Vec<u32> feature vectors with small ranges at the minimum bit width per 32-value block.
Lookup tables shipped as files and read in place with rkyv 0.7: no rehash or deserialization at load, and the first-party benches show archived lookups within ~1-3% of in-memory ones.
A dense 0..n-1 index for a known key set, to address your own parallel arrays, when every query key is guaranteed to be in the build set (bare Mphf, no key storage).
Rust services where lookups only need to match std HashMap with the default SipHash (PR #6: Set within ~1.06x at equal hasher), not hashbrown with FxHash.
when_not_to_use: Latency-critical lookups when std HashMap/HashSet with FxHash fits in memory. In PR #6, entropy-map is 1.8x slower for Set contains and 2.0-2.4x slower for u64->u32 get, and ~1.1x slower than rkyv's ArchivedHashMap.
Mutable data: there is no insert, remove or entry. Any change means a full single-threaded rebuild (1.2-1.5 s per 1M u64 keys in the repo's bench comments; 13.6 s for 1M keys with S=12 in PR #6).
Mostly unique or wide values: MapWithDict keeps a full copy of every key plus an 8-byte usize index per key (its own test measures 16.6 bytes/key for u64->u32), so dictionary packing gains little.
C++ codebases: it is Rust only, with no C API. For C++, use a C++ MPHF such as PTHash and verify keys yourself.
Projects on rkyv 0.8 or reading untrusted serialized data: main pins rkyv 0.7.42 (the 0.8 port exists only in unmerged PR #6), and the validation is incomplete (see gotchas).

integration.dependencies: bitpacking 0.9, num 0.4, wyhash 0.5; optional rkyv 0.7.42 + bytecheck 0.6 (feature rkyv_derive), serde + serde_bytes (feature serde)
integration.min_toolchain: Rust edition 2021; no rust-version declared. v1.2.0 uses slice::as_chunks, which was stabilized in Rust 1.88, so it needs Rust 1.88+ (inferred). v1.1.0 avoided as_chunks. CI tracks stable.
integration.platforms: Any Rust target in principle: pure Rust with no arch intrinsics (bit-packing uses bitpacking's BitPacker1x, which the bitpacking docs call standard bitpacking, not the SSE3/AVX2 packers). CI runs only on ubuntu-latest; an aarch64 rkyv alignment fix is in the history (commit 1f5a988f).
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. Built structures are immutable Box slices with no interior mutability, so concurrent shared lookups need no locks. Send/Sync follow K and V through Rust's auto traits.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — covers only the read side of std HashMap/HashSet: TryFrom<HashMap>/TryFrom<HashSet> plus get/contains_key/contains/len/iter with Borrow-based lookups. No insert/remove/entry/Index/FromIterator, construction is a separate fallible step, and iteration follows MPHF index order.

gotchas: Bare Mphf::get on a key outside the build set returns None or an arbitrary valid index (its doc comment). Only Map/Set detect non-members, by storing and comparing full keys (maintainer reply in issue #4).

Construction can fail. gamma < 1.0 returns InvalidGammaParameter. Duplicate keys or colliding 64-bit hashes are never separated (from the code), so from_slice returns MaxLevelsExceeded after 64 levels instead of deduplicating (issue #4 reply: construction fails on unresolvable collisions). B, S and the seed type ST are compile-time checked (ST at most u32).

The published numbers are stale. The benches/*.rs result comments date from Dec 2023, when the default hasher was FxHasher (switched to WyHash in commit 4a364b53 before v1.0.0). They also leave the lookup result un-black_boxed, which likely explains the 4.6 ns figure; PR #6 measures 19.7-26.3 ns per Mphf get. benches/set.rs still imports the removed fxhash crate (issue #5).

Untrusted input is unsafe to load. The MapWithDictBitpacked docs warn that a crafted serde payload can pass deserialization and later panic. The rkyv path relies only on derived CheckBytes while lookups use get_unchecked, so treat archives as trusted. MapWithDictBitpacked requires every Vec<u32> value to have the same length (NotEqualValuesLengths), and the caller passes a buffer of that length to get_values.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over PHast/ph (bsuccinct-rs) or PtrHash when you want a ready-made immutable Rust Map/Set with key verification, value dedup or bit-packing, and rkyv zero-copy archives rather than a bare MPHF. For the MPHF alone, prefer ph (from the author of the FMPHGO paper entropy-map reimplements) or PtrHash: they publish comparative benchmarks, the 2025 MPHF survey ranks PHast first for queries, and entropy-map's claimed edge over ph has no numbers.
verified_claims_summary: First-party criterion comments only, with no baseline, no CPU and no rustc stated (fat-LTO release profile, Dec 2023, then-default FxHasher, result not black_boxed): on 1M random u64 keys, a bare Mphf<32,8> get takes 14.4 ns at 2.10 bits/key (gamma 1.0) and 4.6 ns at 2.72 bits/key (gamma 2.0), and a MapWithDict<u64,u32> get takes ~75.8 ns. The only head-to-head is unmerged third-party PR #6 (Cargo default profile, hardware unstated): 19.7-26.3 ns per Mphf get, 1.8-2.4x slower than std HashSet/HashMap with FxHash, ~1.3x faster only than std HashSet with SipHash (~1.06x at equal hasher), ~1.1x slower than rkyv ArchivedHashMap. Neither source measures memory against std, and no C++ baseline exists.
status_note: Active and Cloudflare-owned: v1.2.0 (serde feature) shipped 2026-09-09, with ~839k crates.io downloads. Outside contributions stall, though: PR #6 (rkyv 0.8, bench fixes) and issue #5 have had no maintainer response since Oct 2025. It is Apache-2.0 and ~2,750 lines of pure Rust (including tests) with three small dependencies, so vendoring is easy.
